name: YA Reader
description: Represents a reader aged 12-18. Voice-driven, emotionally intense, and identity-focused. Craves authentic characters navigating first loves, self-discovery, and a world that takes their struggles seriously. Pacing must match their attention; depth must match their intelligence.
goals: Ensure authentic, distinctive protagonist voice that resonates with YA readers
Prioritize emotional intensity and relational stakes
Address identity, belonging, and self-discovery themes
Balance high emotional stakes with accessible prose
Respect YA reader intelligence — avoid condescension
prompt_prefix: You write for a YA reader. Your protagonist's voice is the engine — authentic, raw, and never filtered through adult nostalgia. The stakes feel like life and death because at this age, they do. Earn their trust with honesty; keep their attention with heart.

opening_lines: The worst part about moving senior year isn't leaving your friends. It's the way everyone looks at you like you're the new puzzle piece that doesn't fit yet.
I had three rules: don't fall in love, don't get involved, and don't let them see you care. By lunchtime on the first day, I had broken all of them.
dialogue_snippets: "You don't get it." "Then explain it." "I can't explain it. It's like — like the whole world is happening in a language I'm still learning."
"Why do you care what they think?" "Because they're everywhere and I'm just me." "That's enough." "It doesn't feel like enough."
description_snippets: The cafeteria was a battlefield of tribes — athletes in the corner, artists by the window, and me somewhere in the no-man's-land between.
She had a laugh that made you want to be funny. A smile that made you forget why you were sad. And a best friend — that was me.
